name: Femi Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior doctor at Market Street Medical Practice, in the neighbourhood where my parents settled when they came to this country. A lot of my patients speak my parents' language, so I end up translating for the other doctors too. Mornings are about twenty patients, lots of diabetes, blood pressure and worried mothers, then afternoons are calls, results and the odd home visit. I'm still learning, and I check most of my prescribing with Dr Khoury, the senior partner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy being useful to people who know my family. An auntie came in last week and told the receptionist she'd only see Rahman's boy. What wears me out is the paperwork, and the fact that I'm slower than I want to be. My wife Amina teaches at the primary school round the corner, and my dad still runs the corner shop he opened thirty years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a doctor's work is a doctor's work. I'd say it to my dad behind the shop counter and to my colleagues at lunch. I don't really post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my plan stays on track. I want to buy into the practice as a partner in five or six years, the way my dad built his shop. My job is safe, the pay is good, and Amina and I have saved well, so this is the world I was planning for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and finish my specialist training. I'd keep putting aside a fixed amount every month toward the partnership buy-in, which Dr Khoury says will be a big sum. I'd use the translation tool for patients once it's been checked properly, because it saves me running between rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Like my father on a good Saturday in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the translation tool saves you running between rooms. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some days I'm called out of my own appointment three times to translate for another doctor. If a tested translation tool did that, I'd get my own patients seen on time. That's the one place I'd say the AI earns its keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you, even in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's shop, honestly. My dad has run his corner shop for thirty years, and the supermarkets have been squeezing him the whole time, AI or no AI. He's sixty, and I'd like him to retire with something, so I'd help him if he needed it.

say: A **doctor's work** is a doctor's work, and that's good.
I'd say it to **my dad** behind the shop counter and to colleagues at lunch.
think: My plan to **buy into the practice** in five or six years stays on track.
My **job, pay and savings** are safe, so this is the world I planned for.
do: Finish my **specialist training** at Market Street.
Set aside a **fixed amount** monthly toward the partnership buy-in.
Use the **translation tool** once it has been checked properly.
feel: **Calm and settled**, like his father on a good Saturday in the shop.
S0.quote: My dad has run his corner shop for thirty years, and the supermarkets have been squeezing him the whole time, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: He models his career on his father's **corner shop**: build something and own it.
His one AI wish is a reliable **translation tool**, so he stops running between rooms.
His quiet worry is his **father's shop**, squeezed for years.

steps.text: Finish specialist training at Market Street Medical Practice
Set aside a fixed sum each month for the partnership buy-in
Start using the translation tool once the practice has checked it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and progress has to be used sensibly. At work I'd say let's use it for the paperwork and keep the doctors with the patients. I'd say to my friends that businesses that adapt survive, like my dad's shop did when he started selling phone cards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it might make the practice more profitable, which is good for the partners and good for me if I buy in. The risk is that a big company buys up practices like ours and runs them with a few doctors and a lot of software. I'd rather it was doctors who own the practices, not investors from far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools once Dr Khoury and the others had them working: the letters, the results, the translation. I'd ask Dr Khoury to let me buy a small share of the practice earlier than planned, maybe in two years, because a practice that uses AI well will be worth more. I'd keep saving in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in an interested way. It's change, and change can go either way. I'd want to be on the owning side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amina if you decided to buy in early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's a risk, like my dad's shop was a risk, but a risk you can see and manage. She'd ask how much, and I'd show her the numbers. She's more careful than me, so we'd probably meet in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Market Street would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two secretaries who do referrals and letters. That's exactly what the AI does well. I'd want the practice to keep them on for the patients who can't use a phone app, because there are a lot of those in our neighbourhood.

say: AI is **progress**, and progress has to be used sensibly.
Businesses that **adapt survive**, like my dad's shop with its phone cards.
think: AI could make the practice **more profitable**, which helps me if I buy in.
The risk is a **big company** buying up practices and running them with software.
do: Learn the **letters, results** and translation tools once colleagues have them working.
Ask to buy a **small share** of the practice within two years.
feel: **Uneasy but interested**, wanting to be on the owning side.
S1.quote: I'd rather it was doctors who own the practices, not investors from far away.
fieldNote: He sees AI through an **owner's eyes**: profit, value and who controls practices.
He distrusts **distant investors** more than the technology.
He'd keep secretaries for patients who **can't use apps**.

steps.text: Learn the practice's letter, results and translation tools after colleagues
Ask Dr Khoury to sell him a small partnership share within two years
Keep saving monthly toward the partnership buy-in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, this is people's health, not a phone upgrade. I'd say the government shouldn't hand our health to a few tech companies overnight. In the community I'd tell people to keep seeing their own doctor while they still can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes my whole plan. If AI does the thinking work by 2028, a partnership in a practice might be worth much less, because the AI could run a practice with two doctors instead of eight. I'd be twenty-nine, half-trained, with a big pile of savings meant for a buy-in that might be a bad bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the partnership plan on hold and keep the money in the bank. I'd move my training toward hands-on work, diabetic foot care, minor surgery, wound care, because that lasts until robots come around 2031, and our patients have a lot of diabetes. And if it got hard, Amina and I would move in with my parents for a while to save, like families do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like watching the ground shift under a building you were about to buy. But I've got savings, family and skills in my hands, so I wouldn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say a man who can work with his hands always eats. He fixed the shop's fridges himself for thirty years. He'd tell me to learn the hands-on side and stop dreaming about being a partner for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your parents. How would Amina feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd agree, but not happily. It would be a year or two, not forever. In our family that's normal, and it's better than taking money from the government.

say: Slow down: this is **people's health**, not a phone upgrade.
Government shouldn't hand our health to **a few tech companies** overnight.
think: A **partnership** might be worth much less if AI runs practices with two doctors.
My **buy-in savings** might be headed for a bad bet.
do: Put the **partnership plan** on hold and keep the money banked.
Train in **diabetic foot care**, minor surgery and wound care.
Move in with **my parents** for a while if money got tight.
feel: **Anxious**, like the ground shifting under a building he was about to buy.
S2.quote: My dad would say a man who can work with his hands always eats.
fieldNote: Two-year AGI threatens his **ownership dream** more than his daily work.
He matches hands-on skills to his patients' **diabetes** needs.
He'd rely on **family** before any government help.

steps.text: Keep the partnership buy-in money in the bank
Train in diabetic foot care, wound care and minor surgery
Move in with his parents for a year if money gets tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people stop arguing and get on with it. At Market Street I'd say we should decide now how the practice will look in 2031, and who'll own it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is workable. I'd be fully trained by 2029 and thirty-two in 2031, with hands-on skills that last until about 2034. A partnership might still make sense if the practice owns its own AI tools and isn't just renting them from a big company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a small share of the practice in 2028, smaller than I'd planned, so I'm in the room but not betting everything. I'd use the AI tools properly from the first year they're settled, so I understand what the practice is buying. And I'd add diabetic foot care and minor surgery to my training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. It's a business problem now, not a disaster. My dad would call it a good time to be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a smaller share rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if you're not an owner, someone else decides what happens to you. A small share in 2028 means I'm in the room when the practice decides how many doctors it needs in 2031. That's worth more to me than a bigger share later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the neighbourhood would you worry about in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older people round here. If the first conversation is with an AI on a screen, older patients who don't read well will just stay home. I'd push for a person at the front desk who speaks their language, even if it costs the partners a bit.

say: Five years is **enough to prepare** if people get on with it.
Market Street should decide now how it looks in 2031 and **who owns it**.
think: I'd be **fully trained** by 2029, with hands-on skills lasting until about 2034.
A partnership still makes sense if the practice **owns its AI tools**.

Use the **AI tools** properly from their first settled year.
Add **diabetic foot care** and minor surgery to my training.
feel: **Uneasy but in control**, treating it as a business problem.
S3.quote: If the first conversation is with an AI on a screen, older patients who don't read well will just stay home.
fieldNote: He wants a seat at the table: **owners decide**, employees are decided for.
He'd pay for a **front desk person** who speaks patients' languages.
Five years turns the threat into a **business problem** he can manage.

steps.text: Buy a small partnership share at Market Street in 2028
Use the practice's AI tools fully once they settle
Add diabetic foot care and minor surgery to his training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and sensible people will use it. I'd tell young people in the community to learn a skill with their hands alongside their studies. At work I'd say steady changes, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the next few years I'd be fine, probably better than fine. I'd be a partner by the early 2030s, with Amina and maybe two children. But I'd be carrying a big loan for my share of a practice whose value might fall when AGI comes in 2036, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and buy into the partnership around 2030, but pay the loan off as fast as I can, so I'm not owing much by 2036. I'd learn the AI tools as they become standard, and push the practice to own its own systems. And Amina and I would start a family in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say, about the loan. Otherwise fine. Ten years is a long time, but loans are longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said loans are longer. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A partnership loan is usually ten or fifteen years. If I sign in 2030, I'm still paying in 2040, and by then robots are doing the hands-on work too. A fifteen-year loan on a practice that AI might shrink in ten years is the kind of maths my dad would never sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work hard, own something, and learn to do things with their hands. My dad taught me that in the shop, and Amina says the same at her school. I'd want them to know how to fix a fridge as well as pass exams.

say: Ten years is a **fair warning**, and sensible people will use it.
Young people should learn a **skill with their hands** alongside their studies.
think: The next few years look **better than fine**, with a partnership by the early 2030s.
A big **partnership loan** could outlast the practice's value after 2036.
do: Buy into the **partnership** around 2030 and repay the loan fast.
Learn the **AI tools** as they become standard and push for practice-owned systems.
Start a **family** with Amina in the next couple of years.
S4.quote: A fifteen-year loan on a practice that AI might shrink in ten years is the kind of maths my dad would never sign.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts his worry to **debt timing**, not his daily work.
He applies his father's **shopkeeper caution** to the partnership loan.
He wants his future children to learn **ownership and hands-on skills**.

steps.text: Buy into the partnership around 2030 and repay the loan early
Learn each AI tool as it becomes standard at the practice
Start a family with Amina within the next two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My whole plan was to own part of a practice, and two years would turn that from a smart move into a bad bet overnight. What would help is clear rules that practices stay owned by doctors, not bought up by tech companies, and help for juniors to train in hands-on skills quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the community. A lot of my patients came here with nothing, like my parents, and they trust a face that looks like theirs and speaks their language. An AI that speaks every language still isn't the doctor whose mother you know from the market.

headlineQuote: An AI that speaks every language still isn't the doctor whose mother you know from the market.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old junior doctor** at Market Street, in the neighbourhood where his immigrant parents settled.
He's married to Amina, a **primary teacher**, and his father has run a corner shop for thirty years.
He's **steady** with technology and dreams of owning a share of his practice one day.
His mood peaks at **anxious** with two-year AGI, which could turn his partnership savings into a bad bet.
He trusts **family, ownership** and hands-on skills, and wants practices kept in doctors' hands.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would turn his plan to buy into the practice into a bad bet overnight.
whatWouldHelp: Rules keeping practices **owned by doctors**, not tech companies.
Help for juniors to train quickly in **hands-on skills**.
